title: How to multiply anything with no times table
description:
Egyptian scribes multiplied by doubling. For 13 x 24: write 1 next to 24 and keep doubling both sides (2 and 48, 4 and 96, 8 and 192), then tick the rows whose left side adds up to 13 (8 + 4 + 1) and add their right side: 192 + 96 + 24 = 312. It always works because every whole number splits into distinct powers of two in exactly one way, which is binary, and it is the same shift-and-add idea a computer's multiplier circuit uses. The method is in the Rhind and Moscow mathematical papyri (the Rhind papyrus dates to around 1550 BC, copied by the scribe Ahmes).

Numbers checked in code: the table, the sum, the comment puzzle, that every number up to 10,000 splits into doubles one way only, and 200,000 random products. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egyptian_multiplication, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhind_Mathematical_Papyrus.

facts_checked: Ancient Egyptian multiplication: decompose one factor into powers of two, build a doubling table of the other, add the matching rows; needs only doubling, halving and addition; worked example 25 x 7 = 112 + 56 + 7; same idea as binary multiplier circuits (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egyptian_multiplication)

The method appears in the Moscow and Rhind Mathematical Papyri; the Rhind papyrus dates to around 1550 BC, copied by the scribe Ahmes (Ahmose) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhind_Mathematical_Papyrus)
Every n up to 10,000 splits into distinct powers of two in exactly one way; 200,000 random products all correct (verify.py)

beats.say: Multiply any two numbers without a single times table.
No calculator, nothing to memorise. Just doubling and adding.
Egypt, over 3,500 years ago. Your job: 13 times 24.
Step 1: write 1 next to 24. Double both sides. 2 and 48. 4 and 96. 8 and 192.
Step 2: stop before the left side passes 13. The next one, 16, is too big.
Now the clever part. Which rows on the left add up to 13?
Step 3: 8, plus 4, plus 1. Tick those rows. Skip the 2.
Step 4: add their right side. 192, plus 96, plus 24. That's 312, and 13 times 24 is 312.
It never fails, because every number splits into doubles exactly one way. That's binary, and your computer's chip still multiplies like this.
Your turn: 11 times 15. Which rows do you tick?
